John Owen
JON OH-en
proper noun
English Puritan divine (1616–1683); from the Welsh patronymic Owen, a form of Eugene, “well-born.”

See also: John Owen · John Owen

Biblical Definition

John Owen was the greatest of the English Puritan theologians, vice-chancellor of Oxford under the Commonwealth, and the most rigorous defender of definite atonement and the doctrines of sovereign grace that the English tongue has produced. His The Death of Death in the Death of Christ (1647) is the standard Reformed treatment of particular redemption: Christ did not die to make all men savable but to save His own; He laid down His life for the sheep, and the sheep are given Him by the Father. Owen pressed the great question that no universal-atonement scheme can answer—did Christ bear the sins of all men, or did He not? If He did, none can perish; if He did not, the atonement is particular by its very nature. His Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers remains the church’s manual for the daily killing of indwelling corruption: “Be killing sin or it will be killing you.” His Communion with God opened the believer’s distinct fellowship with each Person of the Trinity. Owen was a congregationalist in church order, a champion of liberty of conscience under Cromwell, and a pastor who buried ten of his eleven children. The dictionary honors Owen as the model of Reformed exactness joined to experimental godliness, the theologian who showed that the deepest doctrine drives the warmest devotion.

Webster 1828 Definition

English Puritan divine (1616–1683); supreme defender of definite atonement in The Death of Death and of the believer’s war on sin in The Mortification of Sin.

JOHN OWEN, English Puritan theologian (1616–1683), vice-chancellor of Oxford.

Wrote The Death of Death in the Death of Christ, the standard defense of particular redemption.

Pressed that Christ died to save His sheep, not merely to make salvation possible.

Wrote The Mortification of Sin: “Be killing sin or it will be killing you.”

Joined the deepest Reformed doctrine to the warmest experimental godliness.

Key Scripture

Joh 10:11 — "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep."

Joh 17:9 — "I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine."

Rom 8:13 — "For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live."

Heb 12:14 — "Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord:"

Modern Corruption

Owen is dismissed by modern Arminian and universal-atonement writers as a cold logician, and his demand for the daily mortification of sin is softened into mere self-acceptance.

expand to see more

The corruption is the caricature of Owen as a man of hard logic without warmth, and the wider modern revolt against definite atonement that his Death of Death answered before it was framed. The universal-redemption scheme—Christ died equally for every man, the difference lying only in man’s response—cannot say what the cross actually accomplished without making it accomplish nothing certain. Owen’s argument stands: an atonement that saves no one in particular saves no one at all. The therapy-age also dilutes his doctrine of mortification, turning the believer’s lifelong killing of indwelling sin into a program of self-acceptance that never names sin as sin.

The principle to recover is Owen’s union of exact doctrine and experimental power. He taught that Christ’s death secured the salvation of His people infallibly, and that the same grace which redeems also sanctifies, so that the believer mortifies sin not to be accepted but because he already is. Doctrine that does not drive the soul to holiness is not Owen’s doctrine; holiness that is not built on sovereign grace is not the gospel.

Hebrew Roots

English Puritan (1616–1683); defender of definite atonement and the mortification of sin; congregationalist and pastor-theologian.

John Owen — Puritan divine, vice-chancellor of Oxford (1616–1683).

The Death of Death — the standard defense of particular redemption.

Christ laid down His life for the sheep, not for the world indiscriminately (Joh 10:11).

The Mortification of Sin — the believer’s daily war on indwelling corruption (Rom 8:13).

Joined Reformed exactness to warm, experimental godliness.
